r: SLHS 1500 surveys the science of communication across the lifespan, the culture-communication relationship, and the impact of disorders on individuals and families, while introducing assessment and intervention options at a conceptual, not clinical-skill, level. Much of the applied work is knowledge transmission - summarizing research, explaining frameworks, narrating case examples - which maps to Getting Information and Updating and Using Relevant Knowledge, categories where observed-usage data from the Anthropic Economic Index already shows writing and explanatory tasks prominent. A capable model can already summarize hearing-loss etiology or narrate a language-disorder case study. But the course also supplies the gateway vocabulary every later CSD course assumes, and it carries a GT-Pathways designation fixing it in the transfer core. At 24 months AI assists content delivery without displacing the requirement that a prospective CSD student complete this entry course.

By 2031, AI tools will likely be considerably better at synthesizing communication-science literature and generating illustrative case material, meaningfully raising the automatability of this course's descriptive content; GDPval-style evaluations suggest models are approaching, though not matching, expert performance on this kind of explanatory deliverable. That shift is real for the knowledge-transmission side of the course, and productivity research on professional writing tasks suggests such gains compound quickly once tools diffuse into study routines. What keeps the rating from climbing further is the GT-Pathways general-studies designation, an institutional transfer-core mandate that persists on a slower cycle than AI capability, and the course's gateway role feeding SLHS 2100 and SLHS 3000. The rating moves to Medium primarily because the survey content becomes more AI-tractable, not because the entry-point function within the CSD sequence weakens.

Over a decade, AI explanation and tutoring of introductory communication-science content could become highly capable and widely diffused into study tools, plausibly changing how the survey material is delivered well before 2036, consistent with the fast capability trend documented by METR and Epoch. The open question is how much classroom delivery itself shifts toward AI-mediated instruction versus how much the requirement to complete this gateway course before advancing persists unchanged, and how far diffusion into everyday academic advising and tutoring actually reaches by that horizon. Because SLHS 1500 remains a prerequisite substrate for subsequent required CSD coursework, and the GT-Pathways designation is unlikely to lapse, the rating holds at Medium rather than rising to High even under an optimistic capability trajectory for the underlying survey content.
SLHS 1500.d: The students in this course will be introduced to the science of communication across the lifespan, the relationship of culture to communication, and the impact of communication disorders on individuals and families. Intervention and assessment options for speech, language, and hearing are explored.

r: SLHS 1610 builds basic ASL conversational competence - receptive and expressive signing, fingerspelling, and introductory Deaf-culture literacy - a psychomotor and visual-spatial skill acquired through live, face-to-face practice with an instructor and peers. This sits far from the Computer and Mathematical work the Anthropic Economic Index shows dominating current usage; task-exposure research consistently places real-time embodied interpersonal communication among the least-exposed categories. AI sign-avatar and recognition tools exist but remain far less mature than text-to-text translation, and none substitute for a learner's own hand-shape production, facial grammar, and receptive fluency under live feedback. There is no institutional licensure lock here, but the embodied, in-person nature of language production is itself the protective factor. At 24 months the instrumental need to physically practice ASL with a fluent human is essentially untouched by current tools.

By 2031, machine sign-language recognition and avatar generation will likely be materially better, and translation aids may appear in classroom settings. That expands what AI assists around ASL communication - captioning, glossing, vocabulary drills - but does not substitute for a student's own embodied production and perception, the actual competence being taught. Verification burden matters: judging whether a learner's handshape, movement, or non-manual grammar is correct requires a fluent human evaluator, since subtle errors change meaning in ways an automated system may not reliably catch, the jagged-frontier problem where judgments outside a tool's real competence degrade accuracy. No accreditation or GT mandate anchors this course, so the case rests on embodiment and instructor-mediated feedback, which plausibly still holds at five years, though surrounding practice tools will look different.

Ten years out, sign-recognition AI and generative avatars could be substantially more capable, and it is plausible some receptive practice migrates toward automated tools. The genuine uncertainty is how much vocabulary drilling and self-paced comprehension checking gets absorbed by such systems before 2036. But expressive signing competence - producing fluent, grammatically correct ASL in real time with a live interlocutor, reading non-manual markers, and functioning within Deaf cultural norms - remains an embodied, interpersonal skill AI performs for a learner only as a practice aid, not a substitute for acquiring it. Absent any licensure or GT lock, durability rests entirely on embodiment, which the capability trend so far has not meaningfully eroded; the hedge is wider here than for licensure-gated courses, but the central case still holds Low.
SLHS 1610.d: This course provides students with a basic understanding of American Sign Language including conversational skills and linguistic structures. Students are also introduced to Deaf culture.

r: SLHS 1620 extends ASL I into more complex expressive and receptive fluency - deeper vocabulary, morphology and syntax, and integrated Deaf-culture content - continuing to be an in-person, real-time, visual-manual skill built through live conversational practice. Task-exposure research places this embodied interpersonal production among the least-automatable activities, well outside the writing and coding tasks dominating current AI usage. The course now carries an Oral Communication general-studies designation, adding an institutional transfer-core mandate to the embodiment argument. Automated ASL tools remain immature relative to text-based translation, and even where recognition improves, they assist vocabulary review rather than substitute for a student's own signing competence, which an instructor must observe and correct live. At 24 months neither AI capability nor institutional structure has reduced the instrumental need to take this course.

By 2031, sign-recognition and generative-avatar tools will likely be more capable and may appear as supplementary practice aids, but the course's core deliverable - a student who can hold a fluent, grammatically complex ASL conversation and read the non-manual grammar carrying meaning - remains a live, embodied competence that automated tools augment rather than replace. Verification of correct production still requires a fluent human evaluator; the jagged-frontier finding that automated judgment degrades outside a tool's real competence applies directly to unsupervised signing assessment. The Oral Communication general-studies designation continues to anchor the course within the institutional transfer core regardless of tool capability, since that designation changes on a cycle much slower than AI progress. The instrumental case stays Low, resting jointly on embodiment and the gen-studies mandate.

Over a decade, generative signing avatars and recognition systems could mature considerably, and it is plausible some receptive comprehension practice shifts toward automated tools well before 2036 - a real but bounded uncertainty. The expressive, real-time conversational competence this course targets, however, is exactly the category task-exposure frameworks treat as durable: physical production, live interpersonal negotiation of meaning, and cultural fluency a system does not perform on the student's behalf. The general-studies designation is unlikely to be removed within this window, since transfer-core requirements are institutionally sticky. Taken together, embodiment and the gen-studies lock keep the rating at Low even under an optimistic capability trajectory; the wider hedge belongs to how much surrounding practice technology changes, not to whether the live skill is still required.
SLHS 1620.d: This course is a continuation of SLHS 1610 emphasizing expressive language as well as increasing competence with receptive language skills. The course continues to build vocabulary and familiarity with the complex grammar (morphology and syntax) of this visual language. The deaf experience and culture is integrated throughout.

r: This course teaches theories of language acquisition and developmental patterns from infancy through school age, early literacy links, and the interplay of linguistic, cognitive, and social competencies, including diversity in developmental pathways. Much of the applied work is synthesizing research and explaining developmental frameworks - Updating and Using Relevant Knowledge and Interpreting the Meaning of Information for Others - categories where observed-usage data shows writing and explanatory tasks already well represented. A model can competently summarize milestone sequences or theoretical debates today. But the course is a required prerequisite feeding Clinical Phonetics and Principles of Assessment and Intervention, making it foundational scaffolding for the accredited sequence, not a terminal elective. At 24 months, AI assists content review without displacing the requirement that CSD students master this developmental knowledge before proceeding.

By 2031, AI tools will likely be considerably better at synthesizing developmental-language literature and even generating case vignettes for practice, meaningfully raising exposure on the knowledge-transmission side of this course. That shift is real, but the course's binding role is structural: it sits as a prerequisite substrate that the program's clinical courses assume mastery of, and program-mandated sequencing does not restructure on a five-year cycle even as surrounding tools change. Verification burden is moderate rather than extreme - misunderstanding a developmental framework is correctable in later coursework - but the foundational-scaffolding cap keeps the instrumental case from rising past Medium. The rating moves from Low to Medium primarily because the underlying explanatory content becomes more AI-tractable, not because the prerequisite role weakens.

A decade out, AI systems may handle much of the descriptive and explanatory work of summarizing acquisition theory and developmental norms, and it is plausible that instructional delivery leans heavily on such tools by 2036. The wide uncertainty is how much of the course's content-transmission function migrates to AI-mediated study rather than classroom instruction, a real possibility given writing and explanation are positively associated with exposure in task-exposure research. What is more durable is the structural fact that this course underpins the assessment and clinical-phonetics sequence CSD students must complete in order; foundational-scaffolding courses are capped from rising to High regardless of how automatable their content becomes. The rating holds at Medium, anchored by sequence dependency rather than by any confident claim about the discipline's staying power.
SLHS 2100.d: Students in this course explore theories of language acquisition and describe communication and language development patterns in infants, toddlers, preschool-age and school-age children. Students are also introduced to early literacy development and the relationship between language and literacy. The interrelationship between linguistic, cognitive and social competencies in communicative development will be explored. Students gain knowledge on the diversity of communicative development within the context of a pluralistic society.

r: Speech Science covers acoustic properties of sound, the physiology of the respiratory, phonatory, articulatory, and resonatory subsystems, and the analysis of acoustic data using instrumentation, applied to both typical and atypical speech. The acoustic-analysis component maps to Analyzing Data or Information and Interacting With Computers - tasks already substantially automated by spectrographic and speech-analysis software, and Computer and Mathematical work is the largest category in observed AI usage data. Interpreting that data for clinical relevance, though, still requires understanding the underlying production and perception theory the course builds. It is also a prerequisite for Clinical Phonetics, Principles of Assessment and Intervention, and Anatomy and Physiology of Speech and Hearing, anchoring it as foundational scaffolding. At 24 months, automation reaches the measurement layer, not yet the interpretive competence or the sequence dependency.

By 2031, automated acoustic analysis and AI-assisted signal interpretation will likely be considerably more capable and diffused into speech-science instruction and clinical workflows, pushing realized automatability higher; GDPval-style benchmarks suggest models are approaching, though not yet matching, expert-level performance on structured analytical deliverables like this. That raises the base exposure of the course's technical content, and diffusion data implies adoption of such tools in academic and clinical settings will be broader than it is today. However, the prerequisite-substrate role is what caps the rating: this course underlies three other required courses in the sequence, and program structure does not loosen simply because the underlying acoustic-analysis tools improve. The instrumental case moves to Medium - automation credibly handles more of the measurement work - while the foundational-scaffolding constraint prevents it from reaching High.

Over a decade, it is plausible that acoustic measurement, spectrographic interpretation, and even much of the theoretical exposition become highly automatable, consistent with the fast capability trend METR and Epoch document. The genuine uncertainty is whether that automation changes what a CSD student still needs to personally understand before advancing into clinical coursework, versus simply changing which tools perform the routine measurement, and how much instructors choose to lean on such tools in the classroom itself. Because this course remains foundational scaffolding for Clinical Phonetics, assessment coursework, and anatomy and physiology, the foundational-role cap holds the rating at Medium even under an aggressive capability trajectory. The hedge is genuine: if the program restructures around AI-assisted analysis tools the content could shift substantially, but the sequence-anchoring function is unlikely to disappear by 2036.
SLHS 2530.d: Students are introduced to the nature and acoustic properties of sound and sound generation, propagation, and modification. Speech production and the characteristics of speech acoustics as they relate to typical and atypical speech production and perception are explored. Speech production subsystems of respiration, phonation, articulation, and resonation are examined through the analysis of acoustic data, using readily available instrumentation. Theories of speech production and perception are introduced and explored in relation to both typical and atypical speech and voice production.

r: This course examines how communication processes shape health outcomes, from one-on-one exchanges to large-group information campaigns, and the roles of relationships, culture, technology, and media in health practice. The applied work is substantially writing- and analysis-adjacent - composing health messages, evaluating media campaigns, analyzing communication contexts - activities task-exposure research classifies as strongly positively associated with AI exposure, alongside prominent writing and office-task usage in observed-usage data. A model can already draft health-communication materials or analyze messaging strategies competently. The course is a Social and Behavioral Sciences general-studies course, giving it a GT-Pathways transfer-core mandate that anchors it institutionally regardless of content exposure. At 24 months, the course's conceptual and applied writing content is meaningfully AI-tractable, but the gen-studies designation keeps the near-term instrumental case Low.

By 2031, AI drafting and analysis of health-communication materials will likely be routine, and productivity research on professional writing - faster output alongside quality gains - plausibly extends into this domain, further raising realized automatability of the course's core applied tasks. Verification burden is moderate: health-messaging errors carry real but not acute costs relative to direct clinical care, and this is not an embodied or licensure-gated course. Without a strong foundational role feeding required downstream coursework, the primary brake remaining is the GT-Pathways general-studies designation, which caps but does not eliminate the shift toward Medium. The rating moves up because the content itself becomes substantially more automatable even as the transfer-core requirement persists unchanged and enrollment in the course continues regardless.

A decade out, generative AI is plausibly capable of producing sophisticated health-communication strategy and content approaching the human-expert benchmarks GDPval-style evaluations describe, and diffusion into health-communication practice, while currently uneven per Census BTOS adoption data, would likely be further along by 2036. The genuine uncertainty is how much the discipline itself reorganizes around AI-generated messaging versus how much human judgment remains necessary for culturally sensitive framing, a real open question that this framework cannot confidently resolve. What is more certain is that the GT-Pathways general-studies designation continues to require this content area in the transfer core, which keeps the instrumental case at Medium rather than High regardless of how automatable the applied tasks become, and regardless of how the surrounding health-communication labor market itself evolves.
SLHS 2990.d: Students in this course explore the essential connections between communication processes and human health. Different modes of communication are considered in contexts that range from one-on-one conversations to information exchange with large groups. The importance of relationships, culture, technology, and media for health practices is also explored.

r: This course builds a disability-studies framework and vocabulary, then applies it critically to how media represents disability, including communication, sensory, physical, and cognitive disability groups. The core work is critical media analysis and framework-building, closer to the critical-thinking-intensive tasks task-exposure research finds strongly negatively associated with AI exposure than to routine drafting, though the media-analysis and writing component does carry some positive exposure per the same research. A model can summarize disability-studies terminology or describe media tropes, but constructing a critical interpretive argument about representation and power is a more resistant task. The course carries an Arts and Humanities general-studies designation, adding a GT-Pathways transfer-core mandate independent of content exposure. At 24 months the combination of critical-thinking content and gen-studies lock keeps the case Low.

By 2031, AI tools will likely be more capable at surface-level media analysis and can already draft descriptive summaries of representation patterns, nudging the automatability of the course's more mechanical tasks upward. But the interpretive, framework-applying core - analyzing how media constructs disability identity and using that analysis critically - remains closer to the critical-thinking work that stays comparatively resistant, and the jagged-frontier finding that AI users perform worse outside a tool's real competence is relevant to unsupervised critical interpretation. The GT-Pathways designation persists on an institutional cycle unrelated to AI capability. Taken together, the rating shifts to Medium mainly on the strength of increased exposure in the descriptive-analysis component, while the interpretive core and gen-studies mandate keep it from rising further.

Over a decade, AI capability for synthesizing and even critiquing media representation could grow substantially, and diffusion into humanities-adjacent teaching tools is plausible by 2036, though current diffusion data shows AI adoption still uneven across sectors and slower than raw capability growth would suggest. The genuine open question is whether AI-generated critical analysis becomes trustworthy enough that the instrumental case for a student personally developing this interpretive skill weakens meaningfully - task-exposure research's finding that critical-thinking skills resist exposure argues against a confident yes. The GT-Pathways general-studies designation is unlikely to lapse within this window. The rating holds at Medium, reflecting real uncertainty about how far critical-analysis automation progresses balanced against a durable transfer-core requirement that does not depend on that progress.
SLHS 3000.d: This course provides a foundation in disability studies, establishing a framework of terminology for defining disability and understanding the disability experience. Issues related to accessibility of media will also be explored. Students will critically analyze how media represents and shapes perceptions of disability groups, which include members with communication disorders, autism, or deafness as well as other sensory, physical, or cognitive disabilities.

r: Clinical Phonetics teaches the science of speech sounds and IPA transcription as a tool for assessing speech disorders and monitoring therapy progress, including transcribing both typical and atypical connected speech. Automatic speech-recognition and phonetic-analysis tools already assist routine transcription, a task-exposure-relevant shift in the acoustic-analysis layer. But the clinical core - perceptually discriminating disordered speech patterns and making assessment judgments about a real speaker in real time - is an in-person, high-verification task; misjudging an assessment misdirects therapy for a real client. The binding constraint is licensure: this course sits inside the ASHA/CAA-accredited curriculum gating entry to the speech-language pathology pipeline, and its clinical-concepts content is foundational to the courses that follow. At 24 months, ASR assists transcription mechanics without replacing the trained clinical ear the course develops.

By 2031, automatic speech recognition and computational phonetics tools will likely be considerably better at routine transcription and acoustic measurement, meaningfully raising the technical exposure of that slice of the course. That augments rather than replaces the diagnostic judgment at the center of clinical phonetics, because verification burden stays high - an assessment error carries real clinical cost and the failure is not always obvious from the output alone, the kind of jagged-frontier condition where unsupervised AI use degrades accuracy. The accredited curriculum and its embedded clinical-competency expectations do not restructure on a five-year cycle. The course remains foundational scaffolding for the practicum sequence that follows it. The rating stays Low, held down jointly by verification burden, clinical presence, and the licensure-gated program structure.

Over a decade, automated speech analysis could plausibly absorb much of the descriptive transcription workload, shifting course emphasis further toward interpretation and clinical decision-making, a real and substantial change in day-to-day tooling. But the accreditation and licensure architecture governing the speech-language pathology pipeline, and the human clinical judgment it certifies, remains the central binding constraint through 2036 in the base case, since licensure regimes change slowly relative to model capability. The uncertainty is genuinely about how much routine phonetic analysis automates around the clinician, not about whether a licensure-track student still needs the foundational clinical-phonetic competence this course builds. The rating holds Low, anchored by the licensure-gated clinical pathway rather than by any claim that the underlying science resists automation indefinitely.
SLHS 3200.d: Students in this course gain an understanding of the science of speech sounds and the use of the International Phonetic Alphabet as a tool for assessing speech disorders/differences and monitoring progress in therapy. Skills developed include transcription using the IPA to transcribe both typical and atypical speech, for both single words and connected speech. The course also covers the clinical concepts of articulation and phonology and provides an overview of typical speech sound acquisition and error patterns.

r: This course teaches assessment and intervention principles and professional practice issues in speech-language pathology and audiology, applied through case-based clinical scenarios involving clients from varied cultural and linguistic backgrounds. The applied work is diagnostic and treatment-planning judgment under real client variability - Making Decisions and Solving Problems and Assisting and Caring for Others - a combination of clinical reasoning and cultural sensitivity task-exposure research treats as comparatively resistant, sitting closer to critical-thinking and interpersonal-judgment work than to routine drafting. AI can surface reference materials or suggest generic intervention templates, but weighing a specific client's cultural, linguistic, and clinical presentation is the competence being built. The course sits inside the CSD program's assessment-and-intervention curriculum, contributing to the ASHA/CAA-aligned pipeline. At 24 months the instrumental need for this judgment training is intact.

By 2031, AI decision-support tools for assessment planning will likely be more common in speech-language and audiology practice, offering draft intervention plans or evidence summaries. That augments the clinician's process without replacing the judgment of tailoring assessment and intervention to a specific client's cultural and linguistic context, where verification burden stays real - an ill-fitted plan has genuine costs and the mismatch is not always obvious from the plan's surface, echoing the jagged-frontier pattern of misplaced trust. The course's role in the accredited CSD curriculum persists on a slower institutional cycle than tool capability. The rating stays Low, with the dampening effect of high verification burden and embodied clinical practice outweighing the base increase in exposure that more capable AI planning tools would otherwise suggest.

A decade out, AI-assisted assessment and intervention planning could become considerably more sophisticated, plausibly handling more of the template-generation and evidence-synthesis work within this course's domain. The genuine uncertainty is how much that shifts the clinician's role toward reviewing and adapting AI-generated plans rather than building them from scratch, a real possibility given the capability trend. But the culturally responsive clinical judgment this course develops, applied to real client variability, remains a high-verification, interpersonally embodied competence the program's curriculum continues to require of students entering the SLP/audiology pipeline. The rating holds Low through 2036 in the central case, though this is a course where AI-assisted practice tools could meaningfully change day-to-day workflow without changing the instrumental case for taking it.
SLHS 3300.d: Students in this course explore professional issues and assessment and intervention principles and practices in speech- language pathology and audiology. Students apply their knowledge of assessment, intervention, and professional practice by engaging in application-based clinical scenarios for clients with communication disorders or differences from a variety of cultural and linguistic backgrounds.

r: This course teaches the structural and functional organization of the anatomical systems supporting speech, hearing, and swallowing, and how anatomical and physiological changes affect sound perception and production. The applied work is largely factual and explanatory - anatomical structure, physiological mechanism, structure-function relationships - content mapping to Updating and Using Relevant Knowledge and Getting Information, categories with substantial representation in observed AI usage, and a model can already competently explain vocal-fold physiology or cochlear mechanics. This is a lecture-based science course rather than a hands-on cadaver lab, so little embodied protection applies. It is also a prerequisite feeding the program's clinical-phonetics and assessment sequence, anchoring it as foundational scaffolding. At 24 months, AI assists explanation and review of this content without removing the requirement that CSD students master it before advancing.

By 2031, AI explanation and tutoring of anatomical and physiological content will likely be considerably more capable and widely diffused into study tools, raising realized automatability for the course's descriptive knowledge base, a shift consistent with the fast capability trend documented in recent benchmarks. Verification burden is moderate rather than severe, since misunderstanding anatomy at this stage is correctable before clinical application, and the course carries no embodied protection of its own beyond ordinary classroom instruction. What holds the rating at Medium rather than higher is the foundational-scaffolding role: this anatomy and physiology course underlies the clinical-phonetics and assessment sequence, and program structure does not restructure simply because explanatory content becomes AI-tractable. The rating moves from Low to Medium as content exposure rises.

Over a decade, AI tutoring and explanation of anatomy and physiology could become highly capable and commonly used for review and self-study, plausibly changing how this content is delivered well before 2036, consistent with the fast capability trajectory documented by METR and Epoch. The uncertainty is in how much classroom instruction itself shifts toward AI-mediated learning versus how much the requirement to master this foundational content before clinical coursework persists unchanged. Because the course remains prerequisite substrate for Clinical Phonetics and the assessment sequence, the foundational-role cap holds the instrumental case at Medium even if the underlying explanatory content becomes almost entirely automatable. The rating holds Medium, reflecting confidence in the sequence-anchoring function and appropriately less confidence in exactly how the content-delivery mechanics evolve.
SLHS 3530.d: Students in this course will gain a foundational understanding in the structural and functional organization of the systems that support speech and hearing. The mechanisms of swallowing are also reviewed. Students explore how anatomical and physiological changes may impact sound perception and production.

r: Diagnostic Audiology trains students to administer pure-tone, speech, immittance, and advanced audiometric procedures and to interpret findings across auditory disorders, mapping to O*NET's Assisting and Caring for Others and Analyzing Data or Information activities. Computerized audiometers already automate signal generation and threshold logging, giving the course modest observed exposure on the equipment side, but the applied competence is hands-on: positioning a client, verifying calibration, and making the clinical judgment calls that distinguish conductive from sensorineural patterns inside a live testing booth. Task-exposure research classifies this kind of real-time, psychomotor, client-facing work as low-exposure even as adjacent data-logging tasks score higher. The binding constraint is that this technique course sits inside the CAA/ASHA-accredited communication-disorders pipeline students must complete before graduate clinical training. At 24 months, the instrumental need to personally acquire hands-on audiometric competence is intact.

By 2031, audiometric equipment will likely embed more automated threshold-seeking and AI-assisted report drafting, and observed-usage data shows computer-and-analytical tasks absorbing the largest share of current AI use, plausibly extending into audiology data logging. That augments rather than replaces the skill this course builds: verifying test validity, managing an uncooperative or pediatric client, and interpreting borderline results carries real error cost, and the jagged-frontier finding that users misjudge accuracy outside a model's competence zone argues for keeping a trained clinician at the console. The CAA-accredited curriculum structure does not restructure on a five-year cycle, and this course remains a listed prerequisite feeding directly into Aural Rehabilitation and the broader clinical sequence. The instrumental case holds at Low: tools change, but performing and judging the audiometric exam personally persists through the next catalog cycle.

Over a decade, automated audiometry and AI-assisted interpretation could plausibly handle more routine threshold testing, and METR-style capability-trend data suggests the range of tasks models handle competently keeps expanding quickly. Genuine uncertainty exists about how much routine audiometric measurement migrates toward self-administered or AI-mediated testing by 2036. But the accreditation architecture gating entry to audiology and speech-language pathology graduate programs is not projected to relax its hands-on assessment requirements within this window, and diffusion data shows firm-level AI adoption still lagging capability broadly. Verification burden on ambiguous or comorbid presentations remains high, and the interpersonal, in-person nature of client-facing diagnostic testing resists full delegation. The rating holds Low with moderate confidence, anchored by the accreditation structure rather than by a confident claim that testing automation stalls entirely.
SLHS 3600.d: Students in this course will review acoustics of the auditory system and perception of acoustic stimuli. The basic principles and techniques of hearing evaluation are presented including pure-tone, speech, immittance and advanced audiometry. Students explore audiological findings for various disorders of the auditory system.

r: SLHS Internship/Observation places students directly into supervised clinical activities and professional observation within the discipline, mapping to O*NET's Assisting and Caring for Others and Performing for or Working Directly with the Public. This is embodied, in-person work by design: observing or assisting real clients under a departmental mentor, calibrated to the student's current skill level. Task-exposure research consistently finds manual, physical, real-time interpersonal work is low-exposure, and nothing in AI's current deployment substitutes for supervised presence with a live client. The binding constraint is structural: the course exists specifically to accumulate the kind of clinical exposure that CAA-accredited programs and eventual ASHA certification require, and department permission gates enrollment to match supervision needs. At 24 months, no plausible AI deployment reduces the instrumental need for a student to be physically present accruing this experience.

By 2031, AI note-taking, scheduling, and documentation support may lighten the administrative load around a clinical placement, and observed-usage data shows office and writing tasks heavily represented in current AI use. But the substance of this course — being present with clients, absorbing professional norms, and practicing supervised skills under a mentor's real-time correction — is not a deliverable an AI system produces on the student's behalf. Verification burden stays maximal because a mentor must personally observe and certify competence, an assessment that cannot be outsourced. Institutional brakes such as clinical-hour models documented in adjacent health and counseling fields illustrate how slowly accreditation bodies relax supervised-experience requirements, and CAA's structure for this discipline follows the same pattern. The instrumental case remains Low; only the surrounding paperwork automates, not the presence requirement itself.

A decade out, ambient documentation and AI-assisted case review could reshape how observation hours are logged and reflected upon, and capability-trend data implies broad gains in models' ability to summarize clinical interactions. Still, the central uncertainty concerns administrative overhead, not whether a student pursuing clinical certification can substitute an AI experience for supervised in-person exposure to real clients — the accreditation and eventual licensure architecture in this field shows no realistic path to certifying practitioners without accumulated hands-on hours by 2036. Diffusion data indicates AI adoption remains uneven and slower than raw capability across firms and institutions generally, reinforcing that structural change of this kind is not imminent. The rating holds Low with high confidence: this course's entire function is the embodied hours themselves, which AI does not perform on the student's behalf.
SLHS 3980.d: Students participate in experiences related to the Speech, Language, Hearing Sciences (SLHS) discipline. Students may observe professionals and/or engage in supervised clinical activities consistent with their skill level. All experiences are coordinated by an assigned mentor within the SLHS department. Contact the department for more information. Internship requirements vary by department. For information and instructions on finding and enrolling in an internship, contact the Classroom to Career (C2) Hub at [contact omitted].

r: This course develops knowledge of language disorders, delays, and differences across the lifespan and their neurological, cognitive, environmental, and sociocultural contributors, alongside intervention techniques, mapping to O*NET's Updating and Using Relevant Knowledge and Documenting/Recording Information activities. Large language models already synthesize disorder characteristics and draft intervention-strategy outlines competently, a text-heavy task with real observed exposure; task-exposure research finds writing-adjacent knowledge work positively associated with AI exposure. Yet applying that knowledge to differentiate a genuine disorder from a typical difference in a specific child or adult requires clinical judgment the course is explicitly built to cultivate, and this content feeds the CAA-accredited curriculum's required core without being independently licensure-gated. At 24 months, students still need to personally construct this diagnostic reasoning; AI can summarize categories but does not replace the applied judgment task itself.

By 2031, AI tools drafting differential-consideration summaries and intervention plans from case descriptions will likely be common in coursework and early practice, consistent with the automation-leaning usage patterns the Anthropic Economic Index reports for professional writing contexts. That shifts routine synthesis off the student, but verification burden remains real — misapplying a disorder framework to a case with sociocultural or bilingual differences carries genuine error cost, keeping a knowledgeable human in the loop. The course's content stays embedded in the accredited program's required core, a partial-mandate structure that does not restructure quickly. Given rising exposure on the knowledge-synthesis side, the rating shifts to Medium: AI increasingly performs adjacent drafting work, even as the diagnostic judgment competence remains something the program requires each student to build directly.

Over ten years, models could plausibly handle much of the descriptive classification of language disorders from case data, and capability-trend evidence points to continued rapid task-horizon growth. The honest uncertainty is how much of this course's applied differentiation work shifts toward AI-assisted triage before clinician review, versus how much stays a taught human skill; the sociocultural- and bilingual-difference judgment calls central to the course are exactly the non-obvious-failure cases where the jagged-frontier finding suggests overreliance is risky. Accreditation requirements for this content area are unlikely to disappear by 2036, but their emphasis may shift toward interpretation over rote classification. The Medium rating reflects genuine ambiguity rather than confidence that the instrumental need erodes further — the program-mandated core knowledge role persists even as surrounding tasks automate.
SLHS 4100.d: Students in this course undertake advanced exploration into language disorders, delays, and differences, and the neurological, cognitive, environmental, and sociocultural factors that contribute to them. Students are introduced to language disorders that are common across the lifespan as well as intervention techniques and strategies to improve communication functioning.

r: Speech Disorders and Differences covers speech acquisition and disorders — speech sound disorders, voice disorders, stuttering — with attention to biological, neurological, environmental, and sociocultural factors and intervention strategies, mapping to O*NET's Updating and Using Relevant Knowledge and Assisting and Caring for Others. Speech-recognition and phonetic-analysis tools already assist with acoustic measurement, and generative models competently explain disorder categories and draft sample intervention approaches, giving the course real but partial exposure on its knowledge-synthesis side. Distinguishing a genuine stuttering or voice disorder from typical variation, and selecting intervention tools appropriate to a specific client's biological and cultural context, remains the applied judgment task the course builds and that AI does not perform for the student. This content sits in the CAA-accredited curriculum's required core without being independently licensure-gated. At 24 months the instrumental need to build this discriminating judgment is intact.
